2609.22425.abstract: Quantum Gibbs sampling algorithms generalize classical Markov chain Monte Carlo (cMCMC) methods, and prepare thermal states on quantum computers by implementing local dissipative evolution for a mixing time $t_{\rm mix}$. Since quantum measurements disrupt the prepared state, the rate of extracting unbiased information from the system depends on the recovery of the underlying thermal correlations. The corresponding ''Gibbs resampling'' time $t_{\rm res}$ is distinct both from $t_{\rm mix}$ and from the autocorrelation time relevant to cMCMC sampling. We study this problem in effective classical models that emulate disruptive quantum measurements of local observables on extensive subsystems. When such subsystems are chosen randomly, in models with non-local order parameters we uncover a ''resampling transition'' as a function of the fraction of sites $p$ that are measured, from $t_{\rm res}\propto \log L$ for small $p$ to $t_{\rm res}\propto {\rm poly} L$ for large $p$, in systems of linear size $L$. We argue that this transition is generically absent in systems with local order parameters, and relate this dichotomy to one between the coarsening of initial states that break 1- and 0-form symmetries under Glauber dynamics. Finally, we devise a structured fast-measurement protocol that evades slow resampling even with non-local order parameters, while leaving only a vanishing fraction of all sites unmeasured.

However, in current schemes for proofs of quantumness, quantum provers face the risk of being maliciously exploited by classical verifiers. 2609.24266.abstract: Many computational fluid dynamics (CFD) algorithms solve partial differential equations by discretization, resulting in large and sparse systems of linear equations. While iterative methods are widely used to solve these systems classically, most existing quantum linear system solvers target the solution through matrix inversion rather than approximating it using an iterative procedure. In this work, we develop a quantum implementation of the Jacobi method based on quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). By reformulating the Jacobi iteration as a polynomial transformation of a block-encoded operator, the algorithm requires only a constant ancilla overhead with respect to the number of iterations while maintaining a circuit depth that scales linearly with the iteration number. We demonstrate the algorithm for one- and two-dimensional Poisson problems, including the pressure Poisson equation arising in Chorin's projection method for the lid-driven cavity flow. The proposed algorithm provides a promising building block for future quantum implementations of multigrid methods and preconditioning techniques, bringing quantum algorithms closer to established CFD solution strategies.

2609.27519.abstract: Block error rate is a standard metric in finite blocklength (FBL) communication, yet it conflates two qualitatively different failure modes: block confusions, where the decoder selects a wrong codeword, and block erasures, where it declares a loss. Higher-layer protocols treat physical-layer failures as erasures, but this cross-layer assumption lacks FBL justification. We derive a rigorous upper bound and a companion lower-side estimate on the block confusion probability (BLCP) and block erasure probability (BLEP) for bounded-distance decoders over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels at finite blocklength, recasting the coding problem as a geometric sphere packing one. We analyze the sensitivity of these bounds to blocklength and signalto-noise ratio, characterize the envelope of the upper bound, and derive closed-form Chernoff approximations. Extending the model to idle transmission blocks, we bound the false alarm probability (FAP) and show that a block z-channel abstraction emerges from the bounded-decoding geometry. Numerical results confirm that confusion and false alarm probabilities lie far below the error rate constraint, providing quantitative physicallayer support for the block erasure channel and block z-channel abstractions assumed in protocol design.

2609.28368.abstract: We introduce partition functors: algebraic structures indexed by partitions of finite sets and equipped with restriction and transfer maps along refinements. We construct a monad PD on the category of partition functors and on several categories of partition functors with additional multiplicative structure. For a partition ring, exponential elements in its associated completed ring of symmetric functions acquire canonical logarithms after applying PD. This gives rise to a universal exponential relation between multiplicative and additive power operations. For representation rings this can be used to recover the classical relation between symmetric powers and Adams operations, while for Morava E-theory it can be used to recover Ganter's exponential relation between symmetric powers and Hecke operators. We show that the representation rings of products of symmetric groups form the initial partition ring and that, for symmetric monoidal partition functors, the monad PD is closely related to symmetric invariant tensors and the divided power envelope. We also construct a symmetric monoidal partition ring carrying the universal exponential element, so that its image under PD carries the universal exponential relation.

2609.28440.abstract: We determine the optimal universal coefficient in a reduction of multiple to binary quantum hypothesis testing. Specifically, for every finite ensemble in any Hilbert space dimension (finite or infinite), we prove that the error probability of the global pretty good measurement (PGM) is at most four times the sum of the optimal binary error probabilities. By constructing a family of regular-simplex ensembles, we further show that the coefficient four is optimal, even for arbitrary global measurements. This result improves on the pairwise bounds established by Cheng and Liu [arXiv:2606.06246 (2026)] and entails an explicit, sharp guarantee for the standard PGM itself. Our proof is also simpler: rather than constructing sequential measurements and applying a union bound, our proof relies on purely matrix-analytic techniques, combining a direct block Gram matrix analysis of the PGM error and a refined inequality between quantum Hellinger distance and Bures $χ^2$-divergence. Our analysis also yields a refined, one-shot pairwise Chernoff bound and explicit sufficient number of copies for a desired discrimination error.

2609.30037.abstract: Deployment-oriented compression is attractive for resource-constrained brain--computer interfaces (BCIs), but whether it changes adversarial vulnerability remains unclear. On BCI Competition IV-2a, we compare 32-bit floating-point (FP32) EEGNet and ShallowConvNet models with global magnitude pruning and simulated INT8 post training quantization (PTQ) and quantization-aware training (QAT) across nine subjects and three seeds. Simulation provides differentiable quantize--dequantize models for white-box attacks and gradient analysis, while native TensorRT deployment is used for validation. Accuracy-preserving compression does not improve direct robustness: at $ε=0.005$, EEGNet PGD accuracy remains 22--24\% across FP32, 50\% pruning (P50), PTQ, and QAT. However, P50 reduces bidirectional transfer efficiency to 0.963/0.928 (FP32$\rightarrow$P50/P50$\rightarrow$FP32), versus 0.994/0.997 for PTQ; the same trend holds for ShallowConvNet. Gradient alignment shows a corresponding separation, while native PTQ agrees with simulated clean/adversarial predictions in 95--98\% of cases. These results show that direct robustness, adversarial transfer, and deployment efficiency are distinct properties of compressed EEG decoders.

2609.31517.abstract: We present a polynomial-time reduction from the search variant of the linear code equivalence problem (i.e. the search for a linear isometry between the inputs) to its decisional variant. Altogether, this yields a polynomial-time procedure to recover a linear isometry from an oracle for decisional LCE. From a linear-algebraic perspective, our results provide an explicit reconstruction of a monomial equivalence between two matrix representations from oracle access to the corresponding orbit membership problem.

2609.34995.abstract: Models of quantum systems faithfully map system parameters to observations, but the inverse problem of parameter inference from measurement data presents a fundamental challenge: computationally intractable likelihoods due to an exponentially large Hilbert space. Here, we introduce simulation-based quantum system inference, a unified, likelihood-free framework that learns parameter posteriors directly from classical simulation data. The central idea is to pair polynomial-cost classical simulators, such as Pauli propagation and tensor networks, with normalizing flows or other neural density estimators for accurate, reusable inference. A single model, trained once, maps any new measurement record to its posterior in one forward pass---turning per-experiment inference into a fixed, up-front cost. We numerically demonstrate the framework's versatility across Pauli noise learning, quantum error mitigation, quantum state tomography, and Hamiltonian learning, with examples involving 81-qubit shallow circuits and 735-parameter inference. In each case, the approach yields accurate estimates of identifiable parameters, while posterior uncertainty provides additional diagnostics of non-identifiability and indicates where further characterization is needed. Our framework reduces data-acquisition requirements in quantum experiments and accelerates parameter inference, providing a practical route to characterizing and improving large-scale quantum systems.

2609.35580.abstract: Smoothed analysis is a central framework in classical algorithms for explaining the performance of algorithms beyond the worst case, often explaining why algorithms perform well in practice. We initiate a systematic study of its quantum counterpart and show the following results. $(1)$ We show that there is a total function whose smoothed quantum query complexity is exponentially smaller than its classical query complexity. $(2)$ We give near-tight characterizations of smoothed randomized and quantum query complexities for symmetric Boolean functions, unifying the worst-case complexity results of [Beals et al, FOCS'98] and average-case complexity results of [Ambainis and de Wolf, STACS'00]. $(3)$ We study string problems such as pattern matching and edit distance and, in various regimes, give polynomial to superpolynomial quantum speedups. Our main technical ingredients include a near-tight quantum algorithm for $\varepsilon$-approximating the number of collisions between two non-repetitive strings, improving the result of Le Gall and Ng [QIC'22]. Together, our results show that smoothing can reveal larger quantum speedups than worst-case analysis suggests, opening a path towards quantum advantage on more realistic inputs.

Laarhoven-Walter used this heuristic to derive explicit trade-offs between the target radius and query time for bounded distance decoding (BDD) with preprocessing. Ducas-Pulles subsequently demonstrated theoretical and experimental failures of this heuristic and proposed an alternative model conditioned on the target norm. In this note, we prove an explicit asymptotic trade-off for (decision-)BDD with preprocessing in the Haar-random lattice model, without heuristic assumptions. Using moment identities of Siegel and Rogers, we analyze cosine scores over complete dual balls and bound both error probabilities when distinguishing targets planted at a prescribed radius from uniform targets modulo the lattice. Optimizing the dual radius yields a trade-off between target radius and query time that matches the asymptotic prediction from the conditional model of Ducas-Pulles.

2609.37867.abstract: The interval $[1,c]_T$ between the identity element and a Coxeter element $c$ in the absolute order on a Coxeter group $W$ is a generalization of the poset of noncrossing partitions arising when $W$ is the symmetric group. When $W$ is finite, this poset is always a lattice, and it is natural to associate to every element $w\in [1,c]_T$ its \textit{moved space} $\mathsf{Mov}(w)=\mathrm{Im}(w - \mathrm{Id}_V)$ in the geometric representation $V$ of $W$. It has dimension equal to the reflection length $\ell_T(w)$ of $w$, and gives a realization of $[1,c]_T$ inside the lattice of subspaces of $V$. It is an important tool in the study of $[1,c]_T$. When $W$ is infinite, the moved space of an element $w\in [1,c]_T$ no longer has dimension $\ell_T(w)$ in general, and distinct elements may have the same moved space. We propose a replacement for the moved space of an element $w\in [1,c]_T$ in an arbitrary Coxeter group, that we call \textit{absolute moved space} of $w$. This subspace $\mathsf{AM}(w)$ of $V$ always contains $\mathsf{Mov}(w)$ and has dimension equal to $\ell_T(w)$, and distinct elements have distinct absolute moved spaces. This allows us to derive several properties of noncrossing partition posets that hold in full generality, and to show that the natural map from $[1,c]_T$ to reflection subgroups of $W$, which to $w\in [1,c]_T$ associates the subgroup $P(w)$ generated by reflections lying below $w$ in the absolute order, is always injective. 2609.38060.abstract: Computational self-testing gives a classical verifier command over the quantum register of a single computationally bounded prover. We use this framework to construct the first argument system for BQP with quasilinear total resource requirements in the circuit model. Our argument system is based on the learning with errors (LWE) assumption and requires total resources of $O(\mathrm{poly}(λ, \log g)\cdot g)$ for delegating a circuit with $g$ gates, where $λ$ is the LWE security parameter. This is achieved by constructing a new computational self-test for certifying the prover's quantum state and using it to dequantize the efficient verification protocol of Broadbent (ToC 2018). Specifically, this self-test enables the verifiable, random remote state preparation of tensor product states of the single-qubit Clifford observables $σ_X, σ_Y, σ_Z, (σ_Y-σ_X)/\sqrt{2}$ and $(σ_Y+σ_X)/\sqrt{2}$, with constant robustness: the verification error is independent of the number of prepared qubits. This approach was first proposed by Coladangelo et al. (ToC 2024) in the multi-prover setting. We replicate their result in the single-prover setting by applying the compiler proposed by Kalai et al. (STOC 2023)---which turns any nonlocal game into a single-prover argument system---to a modified version of their self-test.

2609.38073.abstract: We study exact learning with membership queries for concept classes $\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^N$, focusing on the relationships among their deterministic, randomized, and quantum query complexities, denoted $\mathsf{D}(\mathcal C)$, $\mathsf{R}(\mathcal C)$, and $\mathsf{Q}(\mathcal C)$, respectively. The two canonical quantum speedups in this model are witnessed by Grover search and Bernstein-Vazirani, leading to the longstanding conjecture $$ \mathsf{R}(\mathcal C)=O(\mathsf{Q}(\mathcal C)^2+\mathsf{Q}(\mathcal C)\log N). $$ We first refute this conjecture by constructing concept classes $\mathcal C$ and $\mathcal C'$ satisfying \[ \mathsf{R}(\mathcal C)=Ω\!\left(\frac{\mathsf{Q}(\mathcal C)^3\log N}{\log \mathsf{Q}(\mathcal C)}\right) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathsf{D}(\mathcal C')=Ω(\mathsf{Q}(\mathcal C')^3\log N). \] The first bound matches the upper bound of Arunachalam et al.~[Quantum'21] up to constant factors, while the second matches the upper bound of Servedio and Gortler~[SICOMP'04]. In particular, this shows that the saving in the randomized upper bound of Arunachalam et al. fundamentally relies on randomness. Apart from characterizing the optimal relationship between classical and quantum query complexity, our results are the first to show that quantum speedups for learning can go beyond the Grover and Bernstein-Vazirani paradigms.

2609.38736.abstract: Searching in a linked list is one of the most basic problems in classical algorithms. Although the nodes of the list come with memory addresses, classically those addresses play no role in the cost of search: one simply starts at the head and follows successor pointers to search for an element. In this paper, we show that the quantum setting is different. Here, the ambient address space from which the list vertices are drawn can itself affect the query complexity. We study the following problem analogous to search in a linked list in the query complexity model: the input consists of an address universe $[N]$, a public start symbol $s$, a successor oracle $f$ whose non-$\perp$ values trace a hidden simple path $s \to a_1 \to a_2 \to \cdots \to a_\ell \to \perp$, and a marking oracle $g$ that marks at most one list vertex. The task is to decide whether the list contains a marked vertex. We prove that both the decision and search versions of this problem for all $N \ge \ell \ge 1$ have quantum query complexity $Θ\!\bigl(\min\{\ell,(N\ell)^{1/4}\}\bigr)$. Thus, quite surprisingly, when $N < \ell^3$ the optimal quantum complexity is $(N\ell)^{1/4}$, which is strictly smaller than the $Θ(\ell)$ cost of ordinary linked-list traversal. This gives a precise characterization of when the ambient address space yields a genuine quantum advantage for linked-list search. We extend our results and give the same tight asymptotic bounds for the natural double linked-list version as well.

2609.40062.abstract: We establish a no-go theorem for a broad class of quantum algorithms for the dihedral coset problem (DCP). We consider the Fourier-sampling and subset-sum-measurement template proposed by Regev (SIAM Journal on Computing, 2004), which is one of the main approaches to solving DCP. Suppose that, after measuring the lower $n-1$ bits of the subset sum, the algorithm discards any $ω(\log n)$ bits from each of the Fourier labels. Then we prove that the algorithm cannot succeed in solving DCP. This shows that any algorithm following this template must make extensive use of the Fourier labels, and thus serves as a useful guide for developing algorithms for DCP. As a main application, we show that the recent algorithm by Simon (IACR ePrint:2026/1591, August 11 2026) does not solve DCP. We show that after the subset-sum measurement, this algorithm can be implemented (up to exponentially-small error) using only the most-significant third of the Fourier labels, and is therefore subject to our general no-go theorem. To help with verifiability, we release Lean 4 code for our results.

2609.40105.abstract: Quantum algorithms can offer substantial computational speed-ups, yet these advantages may disappear once the cost of structure-agnostic classical data encoding is taken into account. Real-world problem instances, however, often possess rich internal structure. This raises a fundamental question: can such structure be harnessed to make quantum speed-ups survive end-to-end cost accounting? Here we show that it can. We introduce a general framework for structure-aware quantum data encoding that compiles compact recursive descriptions of problem structure into efficient state-preparation circuits, translating structural information directly into reduced encoding complexity. For the uncapacitated facility-location problem, structure-agnostic encoding admits a classical dequantization that eliminates the quadratic quantum speed-up, whereas exploiting the underlying problem structure restores this advantage even when state-preparation costs are included. More broadly, the same framework prepares structured quantum states for combinatorial optimization that capture non-trivial relations among constraints, including group balance, conflicts and synergistic rewards, extending previously reported super-polynomial quantum advantages to broader classes of objectives. These results establish exploitable problem structure as a computational resource for quantum algorithms and provide a systematic route towards realizing quantum advantage in data-intensive problems.

2609.40180.abstract: We prove the first non-trivial upper bound for the quantum query complexity of Boolean Matrix Product Verification ($\mathsf{BMPV}$), answering a longstanding open question in quantum query complexity. For $n\times n$ matrices, our upper bound is $\widetilde O(n^{17/12})$, improving on the standard $O(n^{3/2})$ bound obtained using Grover search by Buhrman and Špalek [SODA 2006]. We complement this result by showing an $Ω(n^{5/4})$ lower bound, which improves over the previous best known lower bound of $\widetildeΩ(n^{19/18})$ by Childs, Kimmel, and Kothari [ESA 2012]. Our approach centers on a connection with Orthogonal Vectors ($\mathsf{OV}$), which asks whether an indexed list of $n$ Boolean vectors of dimension $n$ contains two vectors with disjoint supports. In particular, we prove equivalences between $\mathsf{OV}$ and $\mathsf{BMPV}$ and establish the above bounds for $\mathsf{OV}$. We also prove a tight $\widetilde Θ(n^{3/2})$ bound for a variant of $\mathsf{BMPV}$ that asks whether the product contains a given row vector. 2609.40254.abstract: Every square matrix decomposes its underlying Hilbert space into generalized, nonorthogonal eigensubspaces. We show that a quantum computer can perform such an oblique eigenprojection $Π$ given block encoding access to the input matrix. 2609.40345.abstract: We apply Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) to sample from the Gibbs measures of classical Ising spin Hamiltonians. 2610.02103.abstract: Schur sampling is a fundamental primitive for extracting permutation-invariant information from many-body quantum systems and has broad applications in quantum information science. Circuit-based implementations typically rely on coherent representation-theoretic operations such as Clebsch-Gordan transforms, generalized phase estimation, or quantum Fourier transforms over the symmetric group. As an application, we consider quantum purity amplification (QPA), in which multiple noisy copies of a pure quantum state are combined to produce a state of higher purity. We show that the optimal purified state can be obtained by retaining a single designated output qudit and discarding the rest.

2610.03590.abstract: We present a unified framework for upgrading a broad class of cryptographic primitives to support constant-rate certified deletion. Previous constructions require a linear number of qubits per encrypted bit of certified-deletable plaintext. In contrast, we obtain the first constant-rate constructions in the plain model that achieve certified deletion while preserving everlasting security. Our approach applies to a wide range of "all-or-nothing"-type primitives based on BB84-style encodings, including commitment schemes, public-key encryption, attribute-based encryption, and fully homomorphic encryption. Beyond this class, we also obtain constant-rate certified deletion for primitives built from subspace coset states, such as blind delegation, secure software leasing, functional encryption, and differing-inputs iO, and CCA-PKE. Importantly, our framework does not introduce any additional assumptions beyond those required by the underlying certified deletion primitives. Finally, under the hardness of SIS, we show that public verifiability can be incorporated into BB84- and coset-based certified deletion. In combination with our constant-rate constructions, this yields publicly verifiable certified deletion schemes with constant rate.

2610.07820.abstract: Efficient post-quantum cryptography on resource-constrained Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices requires implementations that exploit the target processor architecture while resisting practical implementation attacks. This paper presents an ISA-accelerated and implementation-hardened realization of Ring Binary Learning with Errors (RBLWE) encryption on a commodity ARM Cortex-M33 microcontroller. 2610.07929.abstract: Let $h_n$ denote the complete homogeneous symmetric function of degree $n$, $s_ν$ the Schur function indexed by a partition $ν$, and $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ the Hall inner product. Using a Vandermonde-type determinantal identity, we deduce that the stable value is a signed sum of numbers of vector partitions all of whose parts have entries summing to at least 2. The same method gives a short proof of Brion's stability theorem. 2610.08299.abstract: Pauli decomposition underpins Trotterization, phase estimation, sparse-Hamiltonian simulation, and variational observables, at exponential naive cost. From the character theory of $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^n$, characters $χ_z(v)=(-1)^{\langle v,z\rangle}$ are the diagonal Pauli strings, so any diagonal operator is already Pauli-decomposed. A general operator still needs the shifts: each $X^{\otimes x}$ couples to a character $χ_z=Z^{\otimes z}$, and the products $X^{\otimes x}Z^{\otimes z}$ -- up to phases in $\{\pm 1,\pm i\}$ -- form the Pauli group, the central extension of $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^n\times(\mathbb{Z}_2)^n$ by that phase group fixed by the symplectic pairing. A section of that extension remains a choice: the bare products $X^{\otimes x}Z^{\otimes z}$, or the genuine operators that insert $Y=iXZ$ at every qubit where $x$ and $z$ overlap. As Fourier analysis on an abelian shift-character lattice (a natural DFT), this formulation is not qubit-bound: $(\mathbb{Z}_p)^n$ recovers Heisenberg-Weyl qudits. The fast algorithm is the FFT for the group at hand; on $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^n$ that FFT is Walsh-Hadamard, at cost $O(n\cdot 4^n)$. paulikit is a memory-bounded realization of that qubit transform: peak usage need not materialize the dense $2^n\times 2^n$ operator, unlike prior codes whose $O(1)$ extra sits on that buffer, checked beyond a billion oscillator terms against Work-Span and bandwidth ceilings.

2610.10911.abstract: A rational polyhedron has Chvátal rank at most one if a single round of Chvátal-Gomory cuts yields its integer hull. For such polyhedra, integer feasibility is in NP $\cap$ coNP by a result of Boyd and Pulleyblank from the early 1980s, so it is unlikely to be NP-hard. Whether it is polynomial has remained open since then. We answer this question negatively, under either of two standard assumptions from lattice-based cryptography. First, a polynomial-time algorithm for this problem would solve bounded distance decoding with polynomial factors in deterministic polynomial time, contradicting a widely believed conjecture. Second, assuming the hardness of learning with errors, an average-case analogue of bounded distance decoding, the problem is also hard on average, for an efficiently samplable distribution of polytopes. Both results rest on an elementary sufficient condition: a polyhedron has Chvátal rank at most one if its width is less than one along every row of some unimodular matrix. For our polytopes, such a matrix exists but is hard to find.

2610.10925.abstract: We develop two new general frameworks for constructing finitely generated residually finite groups that possess infinite girth, satisfy no non-trivial group law, and contain no non-abelian free subgroups. While such groups are rare--with known examples including the first Grigorchuk group, Thompson's group F, and certain iterated wreath products--our approach provides a more explicit construction of such groups realized as subgroups of direct products of symmetric groups. We investigate the relationship between the girth of a group and that of its finite quotients, leading to the introduction of a "marked" girth criterion, which we establish as a necessary and sufficient condition for infinite girth within the class of residually finite groups. Furthermore, we explore the connection between girth and profinite completions and provide a congruence realization result for infinite girth in linear groups. We conclude by posing several open questions that arise naturally from our results.

2610.12098.abstract: Protecting quantum information from noise is essential for reliable quantum computation and quantum memories. Quantum state purification addresses this challenge by processing multiple noisy copies of an unknown quantum state to produce an output state of higher fidelity. Here we establish nearly tight upper and lower bounds on the non-Clifford resources required to implement the symmetric-projection purification protocol. For $n$ copies of a $d$-dimensional system, we construct a Clifford+T circuit that block-encodes the symmetric projector with operator-norm error at most $ε$ using $\widetilde{O}(n)$ T gates, where the tilde-$O$ notation suppresses polylogarithmic factors in $n$, $d$, and $1/ε$. Conversely, using stabilizer nullity, we prove that any Clifford+T implementation of such a block encoding with error $ε<\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-1/n}$ requires at least $2n-2$ T gates, even allowing arbitrary positive normalization and clean stabilizer ancillas. Taken together, these results establish the nearly optimal scaling of non-Clifford cost with the number of copies and uncover the fundamental resource requirements for coherent symmetry projection in quantum state purification.

2610.12357.abstract: We study two problems: Local Leakage Resilience (LLR) for Shamir secret sharing, and worst-case Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI). Both problems concern polynomials $Q(X)$ of degree less than $k$, over a prime-order finite field $\mathbb{F}_p$. In LLR for Shamir secret sharing, one asks how much one can learn about $Q(0)$ given a few bits leaked from each of $Q(α_1), \ldots, Q(α_n)$, for distinct non-zero evaluation points $α_i \in \mathbb{F}_p$. In OPI, one is given input list $S_1, \ldots, S_n \subset \mathbb{F}_p$, and wants to find a polynomial $Q(X)$ of degree less than $k$ so that $Q(α_i) \in S_i$ for as many $i$ as possible. Leveraging recent connection between these two problems due to (Sun, Wootters 2026), we improve the state-of-the-art for both problems. For LLR, we show that there is some constant $δ> 0$ so that, as long as $R := k/n \geq 1/2 - δ$, Shamir secret-sharing is one-bit locally leakage resilient (meaning that one can learn only a negligible amount about $Q(0)$). 2610.12912.abstract: A classic problem in additive number theory asks whether a given subset of integers has more sums or differences. This inquiry naturally extends to finite groups, where one compares the sizes of the product set $AA$ and the quotient set $AA^{-1}$ for a subset $A \subseteq G$. A finite group is considered product-dominant if it contains a higher proportion of subsets where $|AA| > |AA^{-1}|$, and quotient-dominant if the reverse is true. We establish statistical criteria to determine the dominance behavior of large finite groups by analyzing the moments of the random variable $d(A) := |AA| - |AA^{-1}|$. By translating product and quotient relationships into graph-theoretic constructions, we compute these moments through counting independent sets. Our main result demonstrates that for a growing sequence of finite groups $G_k$ with center size $Z_k$ and involution count $T_k$, the condition $Z_k = o(T_k)$ implies the groups are eventually product-dominant. Conversely, if $T_k \cdot \sqrt{3}^{R_k/Z_k} = o(Z_k)$ (where $R_k$ denotes the number of elements whose square is central), the groups are eventually quotient-dominant. Using these asymptotic conditions, we resolve the Miller--Vissuet conjecture by proving that all dihedral groups $D_n$ for $n \geq 3$ are product-dominant. 2610.12913.abstract: The Noisy Linear Equations problem involves finding the solution to a random linear system over a finite field given noisy evaluations. This is a generalisation of various learning problems widely used in cryptography, including Learning with Errors (LWE), Learning with Rounding (LWR), and Learning Parity with Noise (LPN). We present a new sample-preserving search-to-decision reduction for Noisy Linear Equations that has complexity $\mathrm{poly}(n,m,\log q, q/σ)$, where $n$ is the dimension of the secret, $m$ is the number of samples, $q$ is the modulus, and $σ$ is the magnitude of the noise (defined suitably for the kind of noise involved). In particular, this implies search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR that run in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ even if the modulus $q$ is exponentially large, as long as the noise-to-modulus ratio $σ/q$ is non-negligible. Our reduction works for prime moduli $q$. If $q$ is composite, it instead produces a list that contains a small multiple of the solution. Prior to this work, known search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR either did not preserve the parameters of the problem (i.e., $m$, $n$, $σ$, and $q$), or had complexity that scaled polynomially with either $σ$ or the largest prime factor of $q$.

2610.13250.abstract: The Zak phase provides a fundamental geometric characterization of one-dimensional band structures and, when quantized by symmetry, serves as a bulk indicator of polarization and boundary phenomena. 2610.13906.abstract: We study the quantum query complexity of several basic graph problems. 1) We prove a tight $Θ(n^{3/2})$ bound for finding a maximum-out-degree vertex in an $n$-vertex tournament, resolving a conjecture of Mande, Paraashar, and Saurabh [FSTTCS'23]. 2) Using the same proof idea, we give a direct proof that finding a maximum-degree vertex in an $n$-vertex undirected graph requires $Θ(n^{3/2})$ quantum queries, a bound implicit in the work of Apers and Lee [CCC'21]. Both lower bounds above hold even for computing only the maximum degree or maximum out-degree. 3) We also study Maximum $(k,n-k)$-Cut, which asks for the largest cut with one side of size $k$. For every constant $k\geq 1$, we give an $O(n^{2-1/(k+1)})$-query quantum algorithm. 4) We establish a reduction to Maximum $(k,n-k)$-Cut involving $k$-Graph Collision, which asks whether the marked vertices of a known graph contain a $k$-clique. For $k\geq 3$, this yields unconditional lower bounds with exponents strictly larger than $3/2$, showing that this problem is strictly harder than computing maximum degree. Additionally, under a conjecture we propose for $k$-Graph Collision, the reduction yields a lower bound matching our upper bound above.

2610.14380.abstract: Let $κ_p(n)$ denote the maximum kissing number of a lattice $\mathcal{L} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$. We prove that $κ_p(n) \geq 2^{Ω(\sqrt{n})}$ for all $p\ge 1$ and that $κ_p(n) \geq Ω(α_p^n)$ for all $p > 2$, where $α_p > 1$ is a constant depending only on $p$. In particular, our former result improves on the previously best known lower bound of $κ_2(n) \geq 2^{Θ(\log^2 n)}$ for the $\ell_2$ kissing number, which has stood for over $60$ years. (In concurrent and independent work, Laarhoven and Kominers [arXiv, 2026] showed a similar lower bound on $κ_2(n)$ using similar techniques.) In fact, our lower bounds follow from efficient (randomized) constructions of lattices with large kissing number. Our results use a general construction of lattices with large kissing number. Specifically, we show a simple equivalence between such lattices and a new object that we call an exact locally dense lattice. Closely related objects appear throughout the literature on computational lattice problems. Our constructions of lattices with large kissing number then follow as corollaries by showing that constructions due to Bennett and Peikert [RANDOM, 2023] (using Craig lattices) and Aggarwal and Stephens-Davidowitz [STOC, 2018] (using sparsification of $\mathbb{Z}^n$) in fact give exact locally dense lattices, as well as a new construction of exact locally dense lattices built from rotations of the $m$-dimensional checkerboard lattice $D_m$.

2610.15535.abstract: We study the variation of hull dimensions of symplectic linear codes under equivalence transformations preserving the symplectic distance. For a symplectic linear code $C$, we introduce an even-valued invariant $Δ(C)$, which depends only on the equivalence class of $C$. This invariant can be expressed as the generic rank of an associated space of alternating matrices and, equivalently, as twice a corresponding matroid matching number. If $C$ has dimension $k$, we prove that the minimum symplectic hull dimension among all codes equivalent to $C$ is $k-Δ(C)$. Consequently, $C$ is equivalent to a symplectic LCD code if and only if $Δ(C)=k$. We further show that every symplectic MDS code of even dimension is monomially equivalent to a symplectic LCD code. For a symplectic self-orthogonal code $C$, we determine all attainable hull dimensions: for every integer $r$ with $0\le r\le Δ(C)/2$, there exists a monomially equivalent code whose symplectic hull has dimension $k-2r$. We also refine a standard form for the generator matrix of a symplectic self-orthogonal code and derive the corresponding parity-check matrix and the Gram matrix of the dual code. In the self-dual case, we characterize $Δ(C)$ through minors of an associated symmetric matrix. Furthermore, we relate hull variation to graph matchings, establish a bound for $Δ(C)$, and give graph constructions producing symplectic self-dual MDS, optimal, and best-known codes.

2610.15767.abstract: Levenshtein's classical theorem shows that any code that can uniquely decode from \(t\) deletions can also uniquely decode from \(t\) insertions. This symmetry, however, does not generally hold in the list-decoding regime. Several prior results on the capacity and radii of list-decoding from insertions and deletions suggest that insertions are easier to handle than deletions. In an effort to better understand this asymmetry between insertions and deletions under list-decoding, we study an analogous version of McEliece's \emph{average list size problem}. More precisely, given a binary code \(\mathcal{C}\) of length \(n\) that uniquely corrects \(t'\) insertions (or deletions), we are interested in the average number of codewords returned by a \(t\)-insertion (or deletion) list decoder, where \(t' < t\). Focusing on the case of \(t'=1\) and \(t=2\), we find that under two insertions, this quantity is at most \((n+12)/4\) for any VT code of length \(n\), whereas under two deletions it is at least \(n/2 - 10\) when averaged over all length-\(n\) VT codes. The nearly factor-of-two gap between these upper and lower bounds serves to confirm the relative ease of list-decoding of insertions compared to deletions from an average-case perspective.

2610.15955.abstract: A multiple-access channel transmits messages from several senders to one receiver. For quantum outputs, the receiver must distinguish states depending on all messages, while tests for different decoding errors may not commute. In this paper, we give a self-contained account of simultaneous decoding, in which one joint measurement recovers the messages at the established achievable rates using independent codebooks. The proof combines Sen's tilted-subspace method with Cheng's analysis of the pretty-good measurement, a standard measurement for distinguishing quantum states. Auxiliary labels close to a common reference state separate the geometric directions associated with different errors. A Gram-matrix bound then allows separately chosen binary tests to certify the performance of one measurement. The labels are removed from the completed decoder, leading to a deterministic packing theorem that applies to finite state ensembles, including unequal priors. We develop the two-sender case first, with worked examples and figures, before treating any fixed number of senders. Sharper finite-error guarantees for the same decoder are developed separately, with sharp bounds for two specified steps of the analysis rather than a claim of globally optimal decoding. 2610.16719.abstract: Photonic technologies are among the leading platform contenders for demonstrating quantum advantage. Nevertheless, photon losses represent the major hurdle for the realization of a fault-tolerant optical quantum computer, and the need for an accurate characterization of this phenomenon is crucial for classical simulations of quantum algorithms on noisy backends. The noisy regime would require the simulation of the algorithm on a Fock backend or rather assuming the a priori hypothesis on the uniformity of the optical losses, which may lead to wrong predictions about the outcome from the algorithm on a cerain hardware. We propose a Gaussian model that can reproduce a lossy dynamics through the experimental characterization of imperfect interferometers, yielding the corresponding mean vector and the covariance matrix. Such model can be adapted to any continuous-variable architecture (spatial or time-bin encoded) and for both the Gaussian boson sampling or general-dyne based algorithms. Eventually, we quantify the drift of optical losses from being uniform throughout the multiport interferometer by a numerical simulation. This work proposes a blueprint for future characterizations, tailor-suited for specific devices and architectures, as well as for potential error correction and mitigation techniques, and it paves the way for realistic simulations of quantum algorithms on NISQ optical platforms.

2610.16827.abstract: Bastidas et al. (2025) highlighted the importance of exploiting group symmetries to reduce computational overhead and unify simulation methods across both condensed matter physics and ab initio quantum chemistry. I discuss the discrete character transform, which is the group Fourier transform restricted to $Z(\mathbb{C}[G])$, the center of the group algebra, where class functions form a commutative convolution algebra and irreducible characters are its spectral basis. The normalized character table of a non-abelian group can be obtained through a restriction operator, which means an efficient quantum character transform for any finite group with an efficient quantum Fourier transform. I give complementary quantum algorithms for class convolution based on direct class-sum block encoding and spectral implementation in the character basis, explaining their applications to symmetry-adapted many-body dynamics, molecular and spectroscopic symmetry analysis, and quantum walks, as well as characterizing the central information used in hidden-subgroup problems, including its limitations for graph isomorphism.

2610.18482.abstract: Quantum computing promises new capabilities beyond classical computation. Mid-circuit measurements (MCMs) enable error correction and outcome-dependent control, but their reliability is limited by noise on superconducting hardware. These operations depend on accurate quantum state discrimination (QSD), which assigns measured signals to state labels. Neural network-based (NN-based) QSD improves this assignment, yet its error remains bounded below by the Bayes risk of the available readout distributions. A complementary challenge is state deterioration as successive measurements accumulate and circuit execution advances, making static calibration less representative of the workload. We present Lifting, a QSD framework that addresses both challenges through repetition encoding, neural decoding, and in situ calibration. Encoding supplies joint in-phase and quadrature (I-Q) readout signals from the target and auxiliary qubits, while contextual calibration trains the decoder for the conditions encountered during execution. Our theoretical analysis shows that retaining additional channels from a fixed joint distribution cannot increase Bayes risk and establishes sufficient conditions for contraction of an overlap-based upper bound. Experiments across three IBM processors evaluate the framework on repeated stabilizer measurement, parity-check, and teleportation workloads.

2610.18589.abstract: We construct Clifford+$T$ circuits implementing arbitrary $n$-qubit unitaries with worst-case $T$-count $\widetilde{O}(N^{8/7})$ at constant operator-norm error, where $N=2^n$, improving the previous exponent $5/4$. The construction uses $\widetilde{O}(N^{6/7})$ clean ancillas. The main idea is to reduce the data addressed by each query to the block-encoding circuit for a sparse piece while controlling the additional simulation work needed to combine the pieces. We simulate a Hermitian logarithm of the target by flattening its traceless part with a two-layer random similarity transformation, randomly partitioning the transformed generator into block-sparse Hermitian pieces, and combining their evolutions using qDRIFT. For a target operator-norm error $ε\in(0,1/2)$, let $L=\log_2(N/ε)$, the qubit count plus the requested bits of accuracy. By successively correcting the approximation error, we obtain a circuit using $\widetilde{O}(N^{8/7}L^{3/7}+NL)$ $T$ gates and $\widetilde{O}(N)$ clean ancillas whenever $L\le N$. We also prove that, at constant precision, the exponent $8/7$ is optimal within a sequential block-SELECT model.

2610.18777.abstract: We study the randomised and deterministic demand-query complexity of approximate bipartite matching with few query rounds. The demand-query model, introduced in [Blumrosen and Nisan SICOMP 2009; Nisan SODA 2021], is inspired by combinatorial auctions and welfare maximisation, where an oracle returns the first neighbouring vertex (item) of a vertex u (agent) according to a given permutation pi (preference ordering of the agent over the items). For randomised algorithms, our main result gives a trade-off between the number of rounds k, the per-round query budget q=n^{1+δ}, and the achievable approximation ratio. Let 1 <= k <= log n, and -1 <= delta <= 1/k. Every k-round randomised algorithm using O(q) demand queries per round has a worst-case expected-size approximation factor of Omega(n^{1/2k-delta/2}/k). For deterministic algorithms, for k*q >= n, we show that the optimal deterministic approximation factor is ~Theta(n^2/(q*k^2)), thereby improving the previous lower bound of [Nisan SODA 2021] by a polynomial factor over a wide range of parameters. In particular, for q=Theta(n), we improve the deterministic round-complexity lower bound for constant-factor approximation from ~Omega(n^{1/3}) to ~Omega(sqrt n). 2610.18828.abstract: In submodular facility location (SFL), introduced by Svitkina and Tardos (SODA 2006), clients $\cal C$ in a metric space are assigned to facilities $\cal F$. A facility serving a set $S \subseteq \cal C$ of clients incurs cost $g(S)$, where $g$ is a monotone submodular function common to all facilities. The best known approximation factor for SFL is $O(\log\log|\cal C|)$, due to Abbasi, Adamczyk, Bosch-Calvo, Byrka, Grandoni, Sornat, and Tinguely (ICALP 2024), improving on the $O(\log|\cal C|)$-approximation of Svitkina and Tardos. We show that this is best possible up to a constant factor in the value-oracle model by showing that there exists no algorithm with only polynomially many queries to $g$ with approximation ratio $o(\log\log|\cal C|)$. This bound holds for algorithms with unlimited computation time, and when $g$ is restricted to matroid rank functions. We also show that the natural linear programming relaxation has an integrality gap of $Θ(\log\log|\cal C|)$. Our lower bound follows by constructing an extension of Vondrák's symmetry-gap approach (FOCS 2009) for matroid rank functions.

2610.19239.abstract: In this note we explore the following simple question: How does the classic \emph{gambler's ruin} phenomenon change if we allow the gambler \emph{financial leverage}? 2610.19607.abstract: Rising privacy concerns around large language models have accelerated research in private Transformer inference (PTI). Synthesizing the empirical claims in this line of research, however, is hindered by multi-dimensional cryptographic progress and inconsistent evaluation contracts. In this work, we systematize the field by constructing an empirical graph of 62 PTI systems, mapping system attributes to node features and evaluation compatibility to edges. A three-tiered analysis of this graph illuminates the state of private inference. Node-level attribution shows that cryptographic progress drives performance gains across most systems, yet always co-occurs with other factors (model fidelity, hardware, cost accounting). Edge-level auditing shows that only 1 of 1891 candidate system pairs is directly comparable under shared assumptions. Finally, graph-level analysis shows that the scaling frontier of private inference has plateaued at 13B parameters and projects the cost of deploying current PTI techniques on production-scale Transformers. Overall, this graph-based framework equips the community to evaluate PTI claims transparently and channel technical speedups into deployment-scale private inference.

2610.19676.abstract: Encoding quantum information in $d$-dimensional systems (qudits) with $d>2$ offers appealing new directions for resource-efficient quantum computing. However, protecting the coherence of nonclassical qudit resource states remains an open challenge. Dynamical decoupling (DD) is a well-established technique for extending coherence, but its application to qudits is hindered by the quadratic scaling of the decoupling sequence overhead with the dimension $d$. As a result, demonstrations of qudit DD have so far been limited to low-dimensional qudits. Here, we show that noise-biased qudits enable a nontrivial reduction of this overhead, for example, from quadratic to linear. We perform qudit DD on a model $d=8$ qudit, the nuclear spin of an antimony donor in silicon. We benchmark DD performance on highly nonclassical states such as uniform superpositions, cat states, and Haar random states and measure coherence improvements up to a factor $5$ to $10$. For a spin-cat error correction code, continuous DD extends the coherence time of the logical superposition $|+\rangle_L$ to $225$~ms, compared to $19$~ms under free evolution and $85$~ms with a Hahn echo. This improvement shows that DD sequences tailored to a system's noise bias can significantly enhance the lifetime of encoded logical qubits.

2610.21269.abstract: Clean-label backdoor poisoning is a threat to machine learning-based malware classifiers because poisoned samples can be inserted into training data without changing their labels. Previous explanation-guided attacks mainly focus on selecting important trigger features, but the values assigned to these features can also affect the attack behavior. In this paper, we study trigger value selection as an independent design factor in clean-label backdoor attacks against feature-based malware classifiers. We evaluate several value-selection strategies on EMBER 2018 and a Win64 PE subset of EMBER 2024 using LightGBM classifiers. We compare rare-value, SHAP-based, frequency-bounded, co-occurrence-aware, and quantile-based selectors under random and distribution-based malware-similar benign sampling. The results show that aggressive selectors such as MinPopulation and CountAbsSHAP can achieve high attack success rate, especially under distribution-based sampling, but they are also easier to detect by sanitization methods such as Isolation Forest. In contrast, selectors such as CorrCountAbsSHAP and Quantile95 can reduce poison recall while keeping useful attack effectiveness. These findings show that trigger value selection is not merely an implementation detail, but an important design choice that shapes the effectiveness and detectability profile of clean-label malware backdoor attacks.

2610.21273.abstract: We study the problem of online learning of quantum states with logarithmic loss, which is a quantum generalization of online portfolio selection and has applications to quantum state tomography, the task of estimating an unknown quantum state from measurement outcomes. We first establish a regret lower bound, showing that the regret rates of Exponential Weights and the algorithm of Tseng et al. (2025) have optimal polynomial dependence on the dimension. Our analysis leads to two further results. First, our lower-bound proof leads to a quantum state tomography algorithm that is sample optimal up to polylogarithmic factors in the sample size. Second, we develop an algorithm for constructing confidence sequences for the mean of a matrix-valued random variable. A numerical experiment shows that the latter algorithm is competitive with existing methods.

List decoding is incorporated to further facilitate the error performance. Density evolution is performed for the design of the quantization thresholds. Compared to iterative BDD, the proposed scheme requires only moderate increases in memory and computational overhead. Simulation results verify that our scheme outperforms several unquantized soft-aided decoders, while maintaining small memory costs and low BDD attempts.

2610.21357.abstract: We present a fault-tolerant quantum-memory architecture that concatenates four distance-t rotated surface-code patches with the [[4,2,2]] outer code, encoding two logical qubits at code distance d = 2t in a physical footprint of N < 2(2t+1)^2 qubits on a square lattice with nearest-neighbor connectivity. The outer-code stabilizer generators XXXX and ZZZZ, each of physical weight 4t, are measured in situ via verified Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) ancillae distributed through narrow corridors between adjacent patches, without lattice surgery or long-range gates. The outer-code gadgets introduce hyperedge fault mechanisms, but by design each decomposes into graphlike components, so the complete syndrome is decoded by a single minimum-weight-perfect-matching pass. Circuit-level simulations show logical error rates that scale as p^t, consistent with distance-2t protection. Finally, we implement the construction experimentally on a 105-qubit Willow superconducting processor in both the ZZ and XX memory bases. With the correlated-matching decoder, increasing the code distance from d = 4 to d = 6 reduces the block logical error rate by a factor of 1.52. The construction thus provides a near-term testbed for concatenated architectures beyond the standard surface code.

2610.21371.abstract: In this paper we study consistent hashing (a.k.a. sparse partitions) for doubling metrics in the Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model. A $(Γ,Λ)$-hash with diameter bound $Δ$ partitions a metric space into clusters of diameter at most $Δ$ such that every ball of radius $Δ/Γ$ intersects at most $Λ$ clusters in expectation. Consistent hashing has emerged as a central tool in geometric MPC algorithms. However, so far it has been solely used in Euclidean spaces, where it can be pre-computed. On the other hand, in cases where the metric space is received as input and unknown in advance, no previous parallel construction was known. We present the first fully scalable MPC algorithm over machines with local space $n^σ$, that given an $n$-point metric space with doubling dimension $d\leq O(σ\log n)$, samples a randomized $(Γ,2^{O(d/Γ)})$-hash in $O(d/σ^3)$ rounds. There is a dichotomy: if the doubling dimension is $d=Ω(σ\cdot\log n)$, a polynomial number of rounds is required to compute such a hash. We conclude by showing that this MPC primitive yields $O(d/σ^3)$-round fully scalable MPC algorithms for a broad class of fundamental geometric problems in doubling metrics, including stochastic tree embeddings with $O(\log n)$ expected distortion, constant factor approximation for facility location, bicriteria $(O(ε^{-2}),1+ε)$-approximation for $k$-median and $k$-means.

2610.21511.abstract: We determine all imaginary quadratic fields with class number at most 2000, unconditionally: there are 16,453,493 of them, and the largest $|d_K|$ among them is 1,062,350,083. To our knowledge, such a list was previously known only for class number at most 100. We make explicit a recent argument, released by OpenAI and not refereed, that excludes Landau-Siegel zeros: every real zero $β$ of $L(s,χ)$, for a primitive real character $χ$ of conductor $q\ge3$, satisfies $(1-β)\log q\ge5.8\cdot10^{-4}$. An elementary lower bound for $L(1,χ)$ then shows that a field with class number at most 2000 has $|d_K|<1.61\cdot10^{15}$. The fields with $6\cdot2^{28}\le|d_K|\le1.65\cdot10^{15}$ are excluded by Watkins' sieve, and those below are read from the class group tables of Mosunov and Jacobson. As a consequence, the lists of Cremona and Sutherland of imaginary quadratic orders with class number at most 1000, and the counts of Holmin, Jones, Kurlberg, McLeman and Petersen for odd class numbers up to 1999, previously known under the generalized Riemann hypothesis, hold unconditionally. The two steps, the bound for $β$ and the bound for $|d_K|$, are proved in Lean, building on the existing formalization of that argument, and the proofs are checked by two independent kernels. The contributions of AI systems to this work are stated in the paper.

2610.21596.abstract: Robust quantum control usually assumes one of two extremes: the error is of a known form and only its strength is unknown, or nothing at all is known about it. In practice one often sits in between. The size of a static error is unknown, but its class is known, for example, it only shifts energy levels, or it acts on each subsystem separately. We ask how fast a control can cancel, to first order, every error in such a class. A time-independent Hamiltonian can do this if and only if all errors in the class have zero diagonal in a common basis. In that case an equally spaced energy ladder in this basis does it after one period. A lower bound that holds for any time-dependent control with bounded drive power shows that this simple constant control is optimal for several natural classes, including unknown level shifts and unknown local errors on two subsystems. Completely unknown errors need a time-dependent control, and there, knowing the error class shortens the minimum time by a factor $\sqrt{d^2+1}$. So partial knowledge of the error changes not only how long an optimal robust control takes, but also its form.

First, for a discrete mixing distribution, we derive a universal positive-semidefinite lower bound on the Fisher information matrix in terms of the Rényi entropy of order two. We then develop dimension-aware trace bounds using classical Sobolev inequalities. These bounds are expressed in terms of Sibson's $α$-mutual information and yield the scaling $K^{-2/n}$ in dimension $n$. The derived inequalities are further specialized to rotationally invariant mixing distributions supported on discrete spherical shells. In this setting, an intrinsic-dimensional bound on Sibson mutual information leads to lower bounds on the Fisher information in terms of the number of occupied shells. 2610.21761.abstract: A deconfined quantum critical point (DQCP) is a continuous transition between ordered phases with unrelated broken symmetries, beyond the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm. In one dimension, such a transition between a $z$-polarized ferromagnet (zFM) and a valence-bond solid (VBS) is well established numerically in a frustrated spin-$1/2$ chain. Here we ask whether a superconducting quantum processor can resolve this transition and its signatures despite finite-size effects and device noise. The ground states are prepared by ancilla-projected quantum imaginary-time evolution (QITE), whose exact target states are compressed by tensor-network optimization into shallow depth quantum circuits. The hardware data distinguish the phases through their order parameters, spin and dimer correlations, structure factors, correlation ratios, and snapshot distributions. The crossing of the order parameters locates the transition, and its finite-size extrapolation lies close to the thermodynamic-limit value obtained from large-scale numerics. A noise model based on the device calibration accounts quantitatively for the reduced amplitudes measured on hardware. Our findings demonstrate that a Landau-forbidden transition between competing orders can be resolved on current quantum processors.

2610.21874.abstract: Nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) approximates a nonnegative matrix by the product of two nonnegative matrices with a prescribed inner dimension~$r$. The existence of an exact NMF can be decided in polynomial time for every fixed~$r$, and a best rank-$1$ NMF in the Frobenius norm can be obtained from a truncated singular value decomposition. We prove that computing a best rank-$2$ NMF in the Frobenius norm is strongly NP-hard. Our proof uses a polynomial-time reduction from \textsc{Clique} that produces symmetric positive-definite, completely positive matrices with polynomially bounded integer entries. The same reduction also establishes strong NP-hardness of rank-$2$ symmetric NMF.

2610.22023.abstract: In this work we study the application of two-photon correlated quantum states for high-precision time estimation. To achieve this, photon pairs were fed into a Hong-Ou-Mandel polarization interferometer to generate N00N entangled states with $N = 2$. Two- and four-detector schemes were considered, and the achievable time estimation precision of each was studied, with particular emphasis on the system's Fisher information in each case. Our results reveal that using a four-detector scheme, enabling the measurement of both coincidence and photon-bunching terms, achieves the maximum precision given by the quantum Fisher information, without the need of characterizing system losses. We also show that correlations between repetitions arise due to systematic errors, limiting the precision enhancement that can be obtained by increasing the number of repetitions. Taking these correlations into account, we show that the four-detector scheme outperforms the two-detector scheme in the precision of time-delay estimation. With the experimentally determined calibration uncertainties, the four-detector scheme improves the dispersion by a factor of 2 for the repetitions performed, reaching up to a factor of 4 as both schemes approach their systematic floors.

2610.22058.abstract: Let $\mathfrak X$ be a commutative association scheme of class $d$ on $X$. We construct the generalized Johnson association scheme $\mathfrak J_{n,h}(\mathfrak X)$ on partial maps from $[n]$ to $X$ with domains of size $h$. For $1\le h\le n-1$, we prove that $\mathfrak J_{n,h}(\mathfrak X)$ has $(d+1)$-variate $P$- and $Q$-polynomial structures. In particular, its multivariate $Q$-polynomial property answers affirmatively a problem posed for generalized Johnson association schemes arising from finite Gelfand pairs. We also determine the primitive idempotents and the two eigenmatrices, expressing the first eigenmatrix as a product of an Eberlein polynomial and a multivariate Krawtchouk polynomial, and the second eigenmatrix as a product of a Hahn polynomial and a multivariate Krawtchouk polynomial. For the multivariate factors, we use Mizukawa--Tanaka $(d+1,2d+2)$-hypergeometric functions. In an appendix, we identify the normalized columns of the second eigenmatrix with the known spherical functions in the finite Gelfand pair case. We also discuss the orthogonality relations and the imprimitivity arising from partial maps with the same domain, and explicitly describe the multivariate $P$- and $Q$-polynomial structures inherited by the blocks and the quotient.

2610.22181.abstract: We present an algorithm that computes the structural signature and the mean time-to-failure (MTTF) of a monotone binary system at every one of its states, rather than only at the state in which all components work. The exact algorithm is the first to beat recomputation in a nontrivial parameter regime. 2610.22278.abstract: We study the problem of approximately counting subgraphs under local node differential privacy (LNDP), a recently introduced model that enforces strong privacy guarantees in analyses of distributed social networks. We design a noninteractive $(\varepsilon,0)$-LNDP algorithm that, given any public $k$-node template graph $H$, counts occurrences of $H$ in a sensitive undirected $n$-node graph with additive error $O(n^{k-\frac{1}{2}}/\varepsilon^{k-1})$, for any constant $k$. We complement this algorithm with a lower bound showing that every noninteractive $(\varepsilon,δ)$-LNDP algorithm for counting copies of any $k$-node template graph with maximum degree greater than $1$ must have error $Ω(n^{k - \frac{1}{2}})$. Thus, our algorithm achieves optimal error for counting constant-size subgraphs, up to $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ factors. Our results substantially expand the types of network statistics known to be approximable under LNDP: prior work considered only functions of the degree distribution. In addition, our lower bound yields the first known $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ gap between central and local node differential privacy when accuracy is required for all input graphs. Previous separations either only involved $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ factors or only applied to promise problems.

2610.22313.abstract: Recent work of Sawettamalya and Yu (FOCS 2026) initiated the study of \emph{gap-majority} composition in randomized communication. They showed that if computing a $\{\pm 1\}$-valued function $f$ in $r$ rounds requires $I$ bits of information, then distinguishing $\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i,Y_i)\geq 0.01\sqrt{n}$ from $\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i,Y_i)\leq -0.01\sqrt{n}$ in $r$ rounds requires $n \cdot (I-O(\log n))$ bits of information. They also conjectured that the $O(\log n)$-additive ``loss'' can be further reduced to $O(1)$. In this note, we record that a minor adaptation to their approach combining with a finer analysis achieves the conjectured $O(1)$ loss, establishing a gap-majority lemma for bounded-round communication that is optimal up to constant factors.

2610.22318.abstract: The quantum-trajectory description of a noisy quantum circuit is not unique: every Kraus representation of the noise channel defines a different unraveling, i.e., a different ensemble of pure states that averages to the same density matrix. While all unravelings share the same expectation values of observables, they generally differ in the amount of quantum resources carried by the individual trajectories. Here we study non-stabilizerness, or magic, quantified by the stabilizer Rényi entropy, in quantum-trajectory unravelings of Haar-random and $T$-doped random Clifford brickwork circuits subject to local dephasing noise of strength $p$. The canonical unraveling in terms of Pauli jumps is Clifford and leaves magic untouched, so that trajectories retain the Haar-random value of non-stabilizerness. Exploring the full two-parameter family of minimal unravelings, we find that the trajectory-averaged magic can be substantially reduced by a state-independent choice of Kraus operators, and that the optimal choice is not in general the projective-measurement unraveling, but a two-outcome generalized measurement in which the Kraus operators correspond to a weak measurement of the noisy qubit.
